title: Pay £80, Get £100 in Your Pension: Where the £20 Comes From 🫙💷 #shorts
description:
Pay £80 into a pension and £100 lands in your pot.

With relief at source (all personal and stakeholder pensions, and some workplace pensions), you pay in £80 and your provider claims £20 of basic rate tax relief from HMRC. That £20 is 20% of the £100 in your pension, but a 25% top-up on the £80 you actually paid.

If you pay 40% tax, you can claim another £20 back (20% extra relief on income taxed at 40%), so £100 in your pension costs you £60. That extra isn't automatic: you claim it yourself, through Self Assessment or HMRC's online claim.

One thing people miss: even with no earnings, you can pay in up to £2,880 a year and get £720 of tax relief added, so £3,600 goes into your pension.

Sources: https://www.gov.uk/tax-on-your-private-pension/pension-tax-relief · https://www.gov.uk/hmrc-internal-manuals/pensions-tax-manual/ptm044220 · https://www.gov.uk/hmrc-internal-manuals/pensions-tax-manual/ptm044100 · https://www.gov.uk/guidance/claim-tax-relief-on-your-private-pension-payments · https://www.gov.uk/income-tax-rates

Illustration only. 2026/27 rates for England, Wales and Northern Ireland (Scotland's income tax bands and relief rates differ). Relief at source schemes only (net pay workplace schemes work differently). Assumes the £100 sits within income taxed at 40%. Tax relief is limited to 100% of your earnings, or £3,600 gross with no earnings; annual allowance rules apply. General education, not financial advice.
